parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on what the signal wave is changing - it is told that a voltage displacement causes a change in frequency, while the amplitude is described as constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot what is being varied**
Think of the carrier as a fast oscillation that carries the information. Modulation means using the slow audio signal to vary one property of that fast carrier. Here you are told the carrier amplitude stays constant but its frequency is shifted by the signal voltage.

Step 2: **Name the type**
When the instantaneous frequency of the carrier follows the displacement of the signal, with amplitude unchanged, this is defined as frequency modulation, FM.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which property of the carrier is left untouched in this type of modulation and what that means for the variation in amplitude.
Hint 2: Use the given sensitivity of 25 kHz per 1.0 V together with the actual peak voltage of the signal to work out the maximum shift away from the centre frequency.
Hint 3: Remember the frequency does not stay at the shifted value - consider how rapidly it swings up and down, linked to the frequency of the signal wave itself.
parts.proper_answer: 1. zero variation, amplitude remains constant. 2. carrier frequency of $1.2\text{ MHz}$ varies by $\pm 50\text{ kHz}$ (from $1.15\text{ MHz}$ to $1.25\text{ MHz}$) at a rate of $8.0\text{ kHz}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Amplitude in FM**
In frequency modulation only the frequency is altered. The amplitude is deliberately kept constant so it carries no information. So variation in amplitude is zero.

Step 2: **Calculate the frequency deviation**
The sensitivity is $25\text{ kHz}$ per $1.0\text{ V}$. The signal amplitude, which is its peak displacement from zero, is $2.0\text{ V}$. So the maximum shift is: $$\Delta f = 2.0 \times 25\text{ kHz} = 50\text{ kHz}$$ This means the carrier swings $50\text{ kHz}$ above and $50\text{ kHz}$ below its centre value of $1.2\text{ MHz}$.

Step 3: **State the range and rate**
So the instantaneous frequency varies between: $$1.2\text{ MHz} - 0.05\text{ MHz} = 1.15\text{ MHz}$$ and $$1.2\text{ MHz} + 0.05\text{ MHz} = 1.25\text{ MHz}$$ The swing up and down follows the signal wave, so it repeats at the signal frequency of $8.0\text{ kHz}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 4.1 and pick out the tall central line - this is the carrier, while the two smaller lines are the sidebands.
Hint 2: Convert that carrier frequency from kHz to Hz and link wavelength to frequency using the speed of radio waves, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: $\lambda = c/f = 1.25 \times 10^3\text{ m} = 1.25\text{ km}$ for carrier at $240\text{ kHz}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the carrier frequency**
The spectrum shows amplitude against frequency. The large central peak is the carrier itself. That is at $240\text{ kHz}$. The smaller peaks at $225\text{ kHz}$ and $255\text{ kHz}$ are sidebands created by modulation.

Step 2: **Apply c = f lambda**
All radio waves travel at $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$. First convert: $$f = 240\text{ kHz} = 240 \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$$ Then: $$\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^8}{240 \times 10^3} = 1250\text{ m}$$ Convert to km: $$\lambda = 1.25\text{ km}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think of bandwidth as the total width of the frequency spectrum occupied - from the lowest to the highest sideband frequency visible in Fig. 4.1.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the occupied width**
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies that contain the signal. From the diagram the lowest component is at $225\text{ kHz}$ and the highest is at $255\text{ kHz}$. So: $$\text{bandwidth} = 255\text{ kHz} - 225\text{ kHz} = 30\text{ kHz}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Consider how far each sideband sits away from the carrier - that spacing is set by the frequency of the original audio signal.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link sideband spacing to audio**
In amplitude modulation the sidebands appear at carrier frequency plus and minus the audio frequency: $f_c \pm f_{audio}$. Here $f_c = 240\text{ kHz}$ and the upper sideband is $255\text{ kHz}$, so: $$f_{audio} = 255 - 240 = 15\text{ kHz}$$ The same result comes from $240 - 225 = 15\text{ kHz}$. It is also half the bandwidth.
